title: Does Latent Nuclear Deterrence Really Work?
gist: Revisiting his 2025 argument a year later, Matthew Fuhrmann maintains that Germany, the Netherlands and Japan are best positioned to extract deterrence value from nuclear latency without building weapons, because all three can make fissile material yet are credibly not weaponizing. He sets out three conditions for latent deterrence to work — fissile-material capability, credible restraint, and high stakes — and points these threats at adversaries such as China.

insights.claim: Latent nuclear deterrence requires three conditions to maximize success: the means to make weapons-grade highly enriched uranium or plutonium, the ability to reassure others that the country is not bent on arming, and stakes high enough to make threats credible.
insights.speaker: Matthew Fuhrmann
insights.so_what: A three-part screen for judging which non-nuclear states can actually convert enrichment capacity into geopolitical leverage — and which are just bluffing.
insights.quote: The first is having the means to make fissile material — weapons-grade highly enriched uranium or plutonium — a critical ingredient for a nuclear bomb.
insights.locator: The path for countries seeking leverage

insights.claim: Credible restraint is a prerequisite rather than a weakness: a country gains latent-deterrence leverage only if foreign observers believe it does not currently have a Manhattan Project-like program underway.
insights.speaker: Matthew Fuhrmann
insights.so_what: Counterintuitive result — visibly rushing toward a bomb destroys the very leverage latency provides, which reframes how to read enrichment headlines.
insights.quote: However, few (if any) foreign observers believe they currently have Manhattan Project-like programs underway.
insights.locator: All three have the means to make fissile material.

insights.claim: The path to extracting leverage from latent nuclear capability is described as rocky and uncertain rather than reliable, tempering claims that latency substitutes cleanly for weapons.
insights.speaker: Matthew Fuhrmann
insights.so_what: The author's own hedge — latency is a probabilistic edge, not a guaranteed security guarantee, so it will not fully stem proliferation pressure.
insights.quote: The path for countries seeking leverage from latent nuclear capabilities can be rocky and uncertain
insights.locator: The path for countries seeking leverage

themes.theme: Germany, Netherlands and Japan as the leverage cases

insights.claim: Germany, the Netherlands and Japan are the countries best positioned to gain from latent nuclear deterrence, a judgment the author reaffirms a year after first making it despite unfavorable geopolitical shifts.
insights.speaker: Matthew Fuhrmann
insights.so_what: Names the specific states where nuclear-latency signaling should be watched as a live diplomatic instrument, with knock-on relevance for enrichment and fuel-cycle infrastructure.
insights.quote: I argued in 2025 that Germany, the Netherlands, and Japan are particularly well positioned to meet the requirements for success, and I still believe this to be the case.

insights.claim: All three favored countries already possess the means to make fissile material, so observers assume they could build a bomb quickly if they chose.
insights.speaker: Matthew Fuhrmann
insights.so_what: Existing civil fuel-cycle infrastructure is the underlying asset that converts into deterrence leverage — a reason enrichment capacity carries strategic premium beyond electricity.
insights.quote: Given this capability, everyone understands that these countries could build a bomb quickly if they so desired.
insights.locator: All three have the means to make fissile material.

insights.claim: U.S. allies are expected to direct latent deterrent threats at adversaries such as China, positioning nuclear latency as an instrument of allied signaling rather than only a proliferation risk.
insights.speaker: Matthew Fuhrmann
insights.so_what: If allied latency becomes an explicit bargaining tool toward China, it raises the odds of fuel-cycle expansion in Europe and Japan.
insights.quote: U.S. allies could direct their latent deterrent threats at adversaries such as China,
insights.locator: These countries should therefore have better luck

insights.claim: Countries do not always need to actually build nuclear weapons to reap the benefits of nuclear deterrence, an argument the author first made in 2025 and still holds.
insights.speaker: Matthew Fuhrmann
insights.so_what: The core claim: deterrence value can be extracted at far lower cost and political risk than weaponization, which changes how to read threshold-state behavior.
insights.quote: countries don’t always need to go as far as actually building nuclear weapons to reap the benefits of nuclear deterrence
